title: Radical inguinal orchidectomy for testicular tumour
subtitle: Markers first, inguinal approach, clamp the cord before the testis moves

sources.title: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Testicular Cancer

indications: Testicular mass on examination and ultrasound suspicious of a germ cell or other malignant testicular tumour.
Diagnosis, local control and staging of testicular cancer; it is the first treatment in almost every case.
In life-threatening metastatic disease, chemotherapy may start first on the basis of markers and imaging, with orchidectomy delayed, as decided by the MDT.
contraindications: Scrotal approach: never used for a suspected testicular tumour.
Small tumours in a solitary testis or bilateral tumours, where testis-sparing surgery may be appropriate in a specialist centre.
Uncertain diagnosis where frozen section through an inguinal approach could spare the testis.
Life-threatening metastatic disease needing immediate chemotherapy.
preparation: Scrotal ultrasound of both testes; tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG and LDH) drawn before orchidectomy.
Staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, which may be done before or soon after surgery, without delaying the operation.
Offer semen cryopreservation before orchidectomy, and certainly before any further treatment; arrange it urgently if accepted.
Offer a testicular prosthesis, at the same operation or later.

Consent: bleeding and scrotal haematoma, infection, ilioinguinal nerve injury with numbness, chronic groin pain, effects on fertility and hormone levels, prosthesis complications if inserted, and the possibility that histology is benign.
Consider biopsy of the contralateral testis in men at high risk of germ cell neoplasia in situ (small atrophic testis, history of maldescent), per the guideline.
positioning: Supine; the scrotum included in the field so the testis can be pushed up into the wound.
equipment: Soft non-crushing clamp or a rubber sling for early cord control.
Non-absorbable ligatures for the cord stump, absorbable sutures for the aponeurosis and wound.
Testicular prosthesis of the chosen size if planned.
anatomy: The testis drains by lymphatics along the testicular vessels to the retroperitoneal nodes at the renal hilum level; the scrotal skin drains to the inguinal nodes.
This is why the approach is inguinal: a scrotal incision opens a second lymphatic route and contaminates the scrotum.
The spermatic cord runs through the inguinal canal from the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, to the superficial ring.
The ilioinguinal nerve lies on the cord in the canal under the external oblique aponeurosis; the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve runs with the cord.
criticalSafety: Inguinal approach only; never incise the scrotum or the tunica for a suspected tumour.
Control the cord with a soft clamp at the deep ring before handling the testis.
Ligate the cord high, at the deep ring, with the vas and the vessels ligated separately and a long non-absorbable marker suture left for later identification.
Markers drawn before the operation; fertility preservation offered before it.
structuresAtRisk: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Inferior epigastric vessels at the deep ring
Floor of the inguinal canal (creating a hernia)
commonErrors: Delivering the testis before cord control, squeezing tumour cells into the lymphatics and veins.
Low ligation of the cord, leaving a long stump with tumour-bearing tissue.
Mass ligation of the cord, which can slip and bleed into the retroperitoneum.
Not offering sperm banking or a prosthesis.
Breaching the scrotal skin while delivering the testis.
complications: Scrotal haematoma and retroperitoneal bleeding from a slipped cord ligature.
Ilioinguinal nerve injury: numbness or chronic groin pain.
Hypogonadism, particularly with a poorly functioning contralateral testis.
Psychological effects of loss of a testis.
postop: Day case or overnight stay; scrotal support.
Repeat tumour markers after orchidectomy, timed to their half-lives, as the guideline describes, to judge clearance.
Ensure staging is complete and the case is discussed at the testicular cancer MDT with histology.
Check hormone levels and fertility status where indicated; follow up the contralateral testis.
Teach testicular self-examination of the remaining testis.

steps.emphasis: Confirm side with the patient and the ultrasound; record that sperm banking and a prosthesis were offered and the patient's decision.
Markers drawn before the knife; staging planned or done; the operation is not delayed for staging.
Review the contralateral testis: a lesion there changes the plan.
Prophylaxis per local policy, particularly if a prosthesis is to be inserted.
Include the scrotum in the field.
Here the canal is opened, the cord is lifted at the pubic tubercle, and the ilioinguinal nerve is protected out of the way.
The testis is never squeezed or incised; it is handled through its coverings.
Send the testis and cord intact with the cord end marked; never bivalve it in theatre.
Inspect the scrotal cavity and the cord stump; scrotal haematoma and retroperitoneal bleeding from the stump are the important bleeds.
Record the level of ligation, the marker suture, prosthesis details if inserted, and the plan for post-operative markers and MDT.

step.orch.incision.title: Inguinal incision and opening of the canal
step.orch.incision.why: The inguinal approach reaches the cord at the deep ring, where it can be controlled and ligated high, and keeps the scrotum untouched.
how: Make an incision in the groin crease above and parallel to the inguinal ligament, from over the deep ring towards the pubic tubercle.
Divide Camper's and Scarpa's fascia and expose the external oblique aponeurosis and the superficial ring.
Open the aponeurosis in the line of its fibres through the superficial ring, protecting the ilioinguinal nerve beneath it.
pitfalls: Opening the aponeurosis with a deep cut that divides the nerve beneath.

step.orch.cord-clamp.title: Early cord control at the deep ring
step.orch.cord-clamp.why: Clamping the cord before the testis is handled closes the venous and lymphatic exit from the tumour while it is being manipulated, which is the oncological principle of the operation.
how: Dissect the cord up to the deep ring.
Apply a soft non-crushing clamp or a tightened rubber sling across the whole cord at the deep ring.
Only then begin to mobilise the testis.
structuresAtRisk: Peritoneum at the deep ring (indirect sac)
pitfalls: Pulling the testis up into the wound to find the cord, before it is clamped.

step.orch.deliver.title: Deliver the testis from the scrotum
step.orch.deliver.why: The testis comes up into the groin wound within its coverings. Pushing it up from below and dividing the gubernaculum delivers it without a scrotal incision and without breaching the tunica.
how: Invaginate the scrotum with a hand from below to push the testis up the cord into the wound, while gentle traction is applied on the cord.
Divide the gubernacular attachment with diathermy, staying close to the testis and away from the scrotal skin.
Keep the tunica vaginalis intact around the testis.
pitfalls: Diathermy through the scrotal skin while dividing the gubernaculum.

step.orch.doubt-bailout.title: Diagnostic doubt or solitary testis: inguinal exploration and frozen section
step.orch.doubt-bailout.why: Not every testicular lesion is malignant, and in a solitary testis or bilateral disease every millimetre of testis matters. The inguinal route with cord control allows a safe look and a frozen section without compromising a cancer operation.
how: With the cord clamped and the field isolated with packs, open the tunica vaginalis and inspect the testis.
Excise the lesion for frozen section where testis-sparing surgery is being considered, with the agreement of the patient in advance.
Proceed to radical orchidectomy if the frozen section shows malignancy (outside the specialist testis-sparing setting) or is inconclusive and the consent covers it.
Seek senior help and follow the plan agreed at consent.
pitfalls: Opening the testis without cord control or field isolation.
Making an intra-operative decision that the patient has not consented to.

step.orch.high-ligation.title: High ligation and division of the cord
step.orch.high-ligation.why: The cord is the first route of spread. Ligating it at the deep ring removes as much as possible with the specimen, and a long non-absorbable marker makes it findable at any later retroperitoneal surgery.
how: Separate the vas from the vessels at the deep ring.
Ligate the vas and the vessels separately, transfixing the vascular bundle, with non-absorbable ligatures.
Leave a long tail on the vascular ligature to mark the stump and allow it to retract into the deep ring.
Divide the cord distal to the ligatures and check the stump for bleeding before it retracts.
structuresAtRisk: Cord stump (slipped ligature and retroperitoneal haematoma)
pitfalls: A single mass ligature on a bulky cord that slips once it retracts.
Ligation at the superficial ring, leaving a long stump.

step.orch.prosthesis.title: Testicular prosthesis, if chosen
step.orch.prosthesis.why: Many men value a prosthesis, and it is easier to place at the time of orchidectomy. It is a foreign body in a recently operated field, so it is placed and secured in a way that keeps it low and uninfected.
how: Change gloves and confirm the size with the patient's earlier choice.
Place the prosthesis in the scrotum through the inguinal wound, low in the cavity.
Secure it with a suture to the dartos at the scrotal base, and close the neck of the scrotum to prevent it riding up.
Record the type, size and batch.
pitfalls: Placing a prosthesis into a cavity contaminated by a breached tumour or a haematoma.

step.orch.canal-closure.title: Close the external oblique with the nerve protected
step.orch.canal-closure.why: The aponeurosis is the strength layer of the groin; closing it restores the canal and, done carelessly, entraps the ilioinguinal nerve in the suture line.
how: Lay the ilioinguinal nerve back on the floor of the canal and keep it in view.
Close the external oblique aponeurosis with a continuous absorbable suture, recreating the superficial ring without narrowing it.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic before closing Scarpa's fascia.
pitfalls: Catching the nerve in the closure and causing chronic groin pain.
